descripcion_es: Common set phrases in articles, headlines and editorials.
resumen: Figurative set phrases that appear constantly in the English-language press (a U-turn, to tighten one's belt, a double-edged sword). Recognising them is essential for reading editorials; using a few makes a presentation sound natural.

explicacion.texto: The press relies on metaphors from sport, war, sailing and the weather. Many have an equivalent in Spanish, but the image changes: “the tip of the iceberg” is the same, whereas “to move the goalposts” would be translated as “cambiar las reglas del juego” (to change the rules of the game).

filas: a U-turn
a sudden reversal of a decision or policy (es: un giro de 180 grados, una rectificación)
The government made a U-turn on fuel tax.
to tighten one's belt
to spend less money (es: apretarse el cinturón)
Families are tightening their belts.
a double-edged sword
something with both advantages and disadvantages (es: un arma de doble filo)
Cheap credit is a double-edged sword.
the tip of the iceberg
the small visible part of a much bigger problem (es: la punta del iceberg)
These cases are just the tip of the iceberg.
to move the goalposts
to change the rules unfairly while something is happening (es: cambiar las reglas a mitad de partido)
Investors accuse regulators of moving the goalposts.
a level playing field
a situation in which everyone has the same chances (es: igualdad de condiciones)
EU rules aim to create a level playing field.
to kick the can down the road
to postpone dealing with a problem (es: dar una patada adelante al problema)
Leaders kicked the can down the road again.
to bite the bullet
to force yourself to face something unpleasant (es: hacer de tripas corazón, afrontar algo desagradable)
The minister finally bit the bullet and raised taxes.
a wake-up call
an event that makes people realise there is a problem (es: una llamada de atención)
The results were a wake-up call for the party.
to call the shots
to be the one who makes the decisions (es: llevar la voz cantante)
In this coalition, the smaller party calls the shots.
to hang in the balance
to be in an uncertain situation whose outcome is not yet known (es: pender de un hilo)
Thousands of jobs hang in the balance.
to weather the storm
to get through a difficult period (es: capear el temporal)
The bank weathered the storm better than its rivals.
a bone of contention
a subject that causes continuing disagreement (es: la manzana de la discordia)
Fishing quotas remain a bone of contention.
to pay lip service to
to support something in words but not in actions (es: defender de boquilla)
Many firms pay lip service to diversity.
a red line
a limit that must not be crossed in a negotiation (es: una línea roja)
Pensions are a red line for the unions.
back to the drawing board
time to start again from the beginning (es: vuelta a empezar desde cero)
The plan was rejected, so it's back to the drawing board.
to rock the boat
to cause trouble by disturbing a stable situation (es: agitar las aguas, crear problemas)
Nobody wanted to rock the boat before the election.
the elephant in the room
an obvious problem that nobody wants to talk about (es: el problema evidente del que nadie habla)
Debt is the elephant in the room.
to bear the brunt of
to suffer the worst part of something (es: llevarse la peor parte)
The poor bore the brunt of the cuts.
to turn a blind eye to
to pretend not to see something wrong (es: hacer la vista gorda)
The authorities turned a blind eye to the abuses.
to throw in the towel
to give up (es: tirar la toalla)
After three defeats, he threw in the towel.
a lame duck
a leader with no real power (at the end of their term) (es: un dirigente sin poder real, al final de su mandato)
The president is now a lame duck.

items: Headlines leave out articles and auxiliaries: “PM makes U-turn on tax” = The Prime Minister has made a U-turn on tax.
Do not overuse them in a formal presentation: one or two well placed are enough.

ejemplos.frase: Social media is a double-edged sword for young people.
ejemplos.traduccion: Las redes sociales son un arma de doble filo para los jóvenes.

ejemplos.frase: Thousands of jobs hang in the balance as talks continue.
ejemplos.traduccion: Miles de empleos penden de un hilo mientras siguen las negociaciones.

ejemplos.frase: Small businesses have borne the brunt of the energy crisis.
ejemplos.traduccion: Las pequeñas empresas se han llevado la peor parte de la crisis energética.

ejemplos.frase: The referee seemed to turn a blind eye to the fouls.
ejemplos.traduccion: El árbitro pareció hacer la vista gorda con las faltas.

ejemplos.frase: The defeat should be a wake-up call for the coach.
ejemplos.traduccion: La derrota debería ser una llamada de atención para el entrenador.

ejemplos.frase: The water dispute remains a bone of contention between the regions.
ejemplos.traduccion: El conflicto del agua sigue siendo la manzana de la discordia entre las comunidades.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: The government gave a turn of 180 degrees.
This is a sword of double edge.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: The phrase has a fixed form: “a double-edged sword”.

errores_hispanohablantes.mal: The authorities made the blind eye.
errores_hispanohablantes.bien: The authorities turned a blind eye.
errores_hispanohablantes.nota: “Hacer la vista gorda” is “turn a blind eye (to)”.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete the expression (reversal of a decision).
ejercicios.frase: After the protests, the minister made a ___ on the reform.
ejercicios.explicacion: This practises the expression a U-turn from the table, meaning a complete reversal of a decision (es: un giro de 180 grados, una rectificación). Literally it is the U-shaped turn a car makes to go back the way it came, and in the press it is applied to a government that backtracks on a decision. The clue is after the protests: the protests force the minister to back down. The collocation is make a U-turn on something. It is accepted with a hyphen and capital letter (U-turn), in lower case or without a hyphen.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Make a U-turn” = to reverse a decision.
ejercicios.traduccion: Tras las protestas, el ministro rectificó (dio un giro de 180 grados) sobre la reforma.

errores_previstos.explicacion: A turn is just “a turn” (a change of direction or someone's turn); the full expression for a reversal is a U-turn.
A turnaround is a recovery or a positive change (of a company, of a situation), not a political reversal.
Calque of Spanish “rectificación”: in English it means the “correction” of a technical error; the press says a U-turn.

glosario.significado: un giro de 180 grados, una rectificación

ejercicios.frase: With prices rising, many households are ___ their belts.
ejercicios.explicacion: This practises the expression to tighten one's belt from the table (es: “apretarse el cinturón”), that is, to cut spending. The image is the same as in Spanish, but the verb is fixed: tighten, meaning to make tighter. The clue is with prices rising, which explains why households have to save, and the continuous tense are ___ing. Households means family units living together, a term widely used in economics.
ejercicios.traduccion: Con la subida de los precios, muchos hogares se están apretando el cinturón.

por_opcion.tightening: Correct: tighten one's belt is the fixed form (es: “apretarse el cinturón”).
por_opcion.fastening: Incorrect: fasten one's belt means to do up your belt (fasten your seatbelt); it does not have the figurative meaning of saving money.
por_opcion.closing: Incorrect: close means to shut; it is not part of the expression.
por_opcion.squeezing: Incorrect: squeeze means to press hard or crush; there is the noun a squeeze (a tight hold, a restriction: a budget squeeze), but it does not form this expression.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete the expression (to be uncertain, es: pender de un hilo).
ejercicios.frase: The future of the factory hangs in the ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: This practises the expression to hang in the balance from the table (es: “pender de un hilo”): to be in an uncertain situation whose outcome is not yet known. The image is that of a pair of scales that has not yet tipped either way. The clue is the almost complete expression, hangs in the ___, and the subject, the future of the factory, which is what is at stake.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Hang in the balance” = to be uncertain (es: pender de un hilo).
ejercicios.traduccion: El futuro de la fábrica pende de un hilo.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Calque of “pender de un hilo”: in English the image is a pair of scales, hang in the balance. Hang by a thread does exist, but with by.
In the air means “in the atmosphere” or “up in the air” (something that can be felt or is still undecided), but the expression on this card is hang in the balance.
Spelling mistake: it is spelt balance.

glosario.significado: pender de un hilo, estar en el aire

ejercicios.frase: Low-income families bore the ___ of the austerity measures.
ejercicios.explicacion: This practises the expression to bear the brunt of from the table (es: “llevarse la peor parte”): to suffer the hardest part of something. Brunt is a word that today appears almost only in this expression, which is why it is easy to confuse with similar words. The clue is the verb bore (past of bear) and the preposition of after the gap. Austerity measures are measures to reduce public spending, a very common term in economics.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Bear the brunt of” = to suffer the worst part of something.
ejercicios.traduccion: Las familias con ingresos bajos se llevaron la peor parte de las medidas de austeridad.

por_opcion.brunt: Correct: bear the brunt of is the fixed form (es: “llevarse la peor parte”).
por_opcion.front: Incorrect: front means the forward-facing part of something; it does not form this expression.
por_opcion.brute: Incorrect: brute means a violent or cruel person or animal (brute force).
por_opcion.blunt: Incorrect: blunt is an adjective meaning “not sharp” or “frank, direct” (a blunt answer).

ejercicios.frase: The police made a blind eye to the illegal parking.
respuestas: The police turned a blind eye to the illegal parking.
ejercicios.explicacion: This practises the expression to turn a blind eye to from the table (es: “hacer la vista gorda”): to pretend not to see something wrong. The verb in the expression is turn, not make: “make a blind eye” is a calque of Spanish “hacer”. The clue is the preposition to after blind eye, which introduces what is being ignored. The sentence only requires changing made to turned, in the past.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: The expression is “turn a blind eye to”.
ejercicios.traduccion: La policía hizo la vista gorda con el aparcamiento ilegal.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The police made a blind eye to the illegal parking.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: the verb in the expression is turn, not make.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The police did a blind eye to the illegal parking.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Do does not form the expression either: the fixed verb is turn.

errores_previstos.respuesta: The police turned a blind eye at the illegal parking.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The verb is now right, but the preposition in the expression is to: turn a blind eye to.

glosario.palabra: to turn a blind eye to

ejercicios.frase: Foreign companies complain that there is no level playing ___ in that market.
ejercicios.explicacion: This practises the expression a level playing field from the table (es: “igualdad de condiciones”), widely used in trade and competition. The image is that of a flat pitch, where no team has an advantage because of the slope. The clue is level playing ___, which can only be completed with field, and the context of foreign companies complaining that they compete at a disadvantage.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “A level playing field” = equal conditions for everyone.
ejercicios.traduccion: Las empresas extranjeras se quejan de que no hay igualdad de condiciones en ese mercado.

por_opcion.field: Correct: a level playing field is the fixed form (es: “igualdad de condiciones”).
por_opcion.ground: Incorrect: ground means “land” or “floor”; there is common ground (shared opinions or interests), but not in this expression.
por_opcion.pitch: Incorrect: pitch is the football field in British English, but the fixed expression uses field.
por_opcion.court: Incorrect: court is a tennis or basketball court, or a court of law; it does not form this expression.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete the expression (a subject of dispute, es: manzana de la discordia).
ejercicios.frase: The new airport has become a bone of ___ between the two towns.
ejercicios.explicacion: This practises the expression a bone of contention from the table (es: “la manzana de la discordia”): a persistent cause of dispute. The English image is that of a bone two dogs fight over, whereas the Spanish one comes from mythology. Contention means “dispute” or “controversy”. The clue is bone of ___ and the idea of conflict between the two towns.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “A bone of contention” = a subject of dispute (es: la manzana de la discordia).
ejercicios.traduccion: El nuevo aeropuerto se ha convertido en la manzana de la discordia entre las dos ciudades.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Calque of “discordia”: the fixed English expression is a bone of contention; an apple of discord exists, but it is much less frequent in the press.
Spelling mistake: it is spelt contention, with a t.
Contest means “competition”; the expression requires contention.

glosario.significado: la manzana de la discordia, motivo de disputa

ejercicios.frase: Instead of solving the debt problem, the summit just kicked the ___ down the road.
ejercicios.explicacion: This practises the expression to kick the can down the road from the table: to postpone a problem instead of solving it. The image is that of kicking a can along the street without ever picking it up. The clue is instead of solving the debt problem, which contrasts solving with postponing. The fixed word is can, a metal container. A summit is a meeting of political leaders.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Kick the can down the road” = to postpone the problem.
ejercicios.traduccion: En lugar de resolver el problema de la deuda, la cumbre se limitó a darle una patada adelante.

por_opcion.can: Correct: kick the can down the road is the fixed form for “postponing the problem”.
por_opcion.ball: Incorrect: it does not form this expression; kick the ball is literal.
por_opcion.stone: Incorrect: it does not form this expression.
por_opcion.bucket: Incorrect: kick the bucket is a different expression meaning to die (es: “estirar la pata”); be careful not to confuse them.

glosario.palabra: to kick the can down the road
glosario.significado: aplazar un problema, darle una patada adelante

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete the expression (to give up, es: tirar la toalla).
ejercicios.frase: Don't throw in the ___ yet; we can still win.
ejercicios.explicacion: This practises the expression to throw in the towel from the table (es: “tirar la toalla”): to give up. It comes from boxing, as in Spanish, and the image is the same. The clue is the second part of the sentence, we can still win, which encourages not giving up. The only difference from Spanish is the particle in: throw in the towel.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Throw in the towel” = to give up (es: tirar la toalla).
ejercicios.traduccion: No tires la toalla todavía; aún podemos ganar.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Tower is a tall building; the word in the expression is towel (es: “toalla”).
Napkin is the cloth or paper used at meals; the expression for giving up uses towel.
Spelling mistake: “toalla” is spelt towel, with an e.

ejercicios.frase: Low interest rates are a sword of double edge for savers.
respuestas: Low interest rates are a double-edged sword for savers.
Low interest rates are a double edged sword for savers.
ejercicios.explicacion: This practises the expression a double-edged sword from the table (es: “un arma de doble filo”): something with both advantages and disadvantages. It is a fixed formula in which the compound adjective double-edged goes before sword, like all English adjectives. “A sword of double edge” copies the Spanish word order. It is accepted with or without a hyphen, although the hyphen is normal.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los tipos de interés bajos son un arma de doble filo para los ahorradores.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Low interest rates are a sword of double edge for savers.
errores_previstos.explicacion: This is the uncorrected sentence: the fixed form is a double-edged sword, with the adjective first.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Low interest rates are a double-edge sword for savers.
errores_previstos.explicacion: The compound adjective takes -ed: double-edged.

errores_previstos.respuesta: Low interest rates are a weapon of double edge for savers.
errores_previstos.explicacion: Calque of “arma de doble filo”: in English the image is a sword, a double-edged sword.

ejercicios.frase: The poor results were a ___ for the management.
ejercicios.explicacion: This practises the expression a wake-up call from the table (es: “una llamada de atención”): a warning that forces people to react. Literally it is the call a hotel makes to wake you up. The clue is the subject, the poor results, which act as a warning, and for the management, the people running the company. The fixed form has a hyphen: wake-up.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “A wake-up call” = a warning that forces a reaction.
ejercicios.traduccion: Los malos resultados fueron una llamada de atención para la dirección.

por_opcion.wake-up call: Correct: a wake-up call is the fixed expression (es: “llamada de atención”).
por_opcion.wake call: Incorrect: it does not exist; the particle up is missing.
por_opcion.alarm call: Incorrect: alarm call is literally a hotel's wake-up service or an animal's warning cry; it does not have the figurative meaning of a warning.
por_opcion.rising call: Incorrect: it does not exist; rising means “increasing”.

glosario.significado: una llamada de atención, un toque de atención

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete the expression (to get through a difficult time, es: capear el temporal).
ejercicios.frase: The airline managed to ___ the storm thanks to state aid.
ejercicios.explicacion: This practises the expression to weather the storm from the table (es: “capear el temporal”): to get through a difficult period. Weather, which is normally the noun for the conditions outside, is here a verb meaning “to withstand, to endure”. The clue is managed to ___ the storm and thanks to state aid, which explains how it was achieved. Ride out the storm, which means the same, is also accepted.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Weather the storm” = to get through a difficult period.
ejercicios.traduccion: La aerolínea consiguió capear el temporal gracias a las ayudas públicas.

errores_previstos.explicacion: Common spelling mistake: whether is the conjunction (es: “si”); the verb is weather.
Calque of “capear”: in English a cape is a cloak or a headland; the verb in the expression is weather.
Survive the storm is understood literally, but it is not the fixed expression; we say weather (or ride out) the storm.

ejercicios.frase: The committee rejected the design, so it's back to the drawing ___.
ejercicios.explicacion: This practises the expression back to the drawing board from the table: time to start again from scratch (es: “vuelta a empezar desde cero”). The image is that of an architect's or engineer's drawing board, which you must go back to in order to redo the project. The clue is rejected the design: if the design is rejected, it has to be redone. The fixed word is board.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Back to the drawing board” = start again.
ejercicios.traduccion: El comité rechazó el diseño, así que toca volver a empezar desde cero.

por_opcion.board: Correct: back to the drawing board is the fixed form.
por_opcion.table: Incorrect: table is a piece of furniture; drawing table exists, but not in this expression.
por_opcion.desk: Incorrect: desk is a table for working at; it does not form the expression.
por_opcion.paper: Incorrect: it does not form the expression, although on paper means “in theory”.

ejercicios.enunciado: Complete the expression (to support only in words, es: defender de boquilla).
ejercicios.frase: Many politicians pay ___ service to the environment.
ejercicios.explicacion: This practises the expression to pay lip service to from the table (es: “defender de boquilla”): to support something only in words, without action. Lip is part of the mouth: it is a service given only with the lips. The clue is pay ___ service to, with the whole fixed structure except the gap. It is very useful for criticising statements that are not followed by measures.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “Pay lip service to” = to support only in words.
ejercicios.traduccion: Muchos políticos defienden el medio ambiente solo de boquilla.

errores_previstos.explicacion: The expression uses the singular: lip service.
Calque of “de boquilla”: the English expression uses lip, not mouth.
Pay lip service exists, not “pay word service”; the fixed word is lip.

glosario.significado: defender de boquilla, apoyar solo de palabra

respuestas: These cases are just the tip of the iceberg
ejercicios.explicacion: This practises the expression the tip of the iceberg from the table, which is the same as in Spanish (es: “la punta del iceberg”): what is visible is only a small part of a bigger problem. The clue for the order is the structure subject (These cases) + verb (are) + just + complement (the tip of the iceberg). Just, meaning “only”, goes right before what it modifies, the expression.
ejercicios.explicacion_breve: “The tip of the iceberg” = a small visible part of a bigger problem.
ejercicios.traduccion: Estos casos son solo la punta del iceberg.

errores_previstos.respuesta: These cases are the just tip of the iceberg
errores_previstos.explicacion: Just cannot go between the article and the noun; it goes before the tip.

errores_previstos.respuesta: These cases are just the iceberg of the tip
errores_previstos.explicacion: The expression has been reversed: it is the tip of the iceberg.

errores_previstos.respuesta: These cases just are the tip of the iceberg
errores_previstos.explicacion: With be, just goes after the verb: are just.

descripcion_larga_es: Figurative set phrases that the English-language press uses constantly: a U-turn, to tighten one's belt, a level playing field, to kick the can down the road. Recognising them is essential for understanding editorials and articles on economics and politics, and using one or two well placed makes a presentation sound natural. They are difficult because they are fixed formulas: changing a single word (“a sword of double edge”) breaks them.

contexto.que_es: They are idiomatic expressions: groups of words with a figurative meaning that cannot be worked out from each word and whose form is fixed (bear the brunt of, a bone of contention, pay lip service to). The press uses them to make headlines and analysis lively, often with metaphors from sport, war, sailing or the weather.
contexto.por_que_importa: Without them, many headlines and paragraphs in The Economist or the Financial Times remain opaque even if you understand every word. In a C1-level oral exam, a well-used expression (a double-edged sword, a wake-up call) shows command of the language; a badly built one gives away the translation. That is why the exact form matters, not just the meaning.
contexto.cuando_se_usa: In opinion pieces, economic and political analysis and oral presentations on current affairs. The signals are contexts of crisis, negotiation, reform or conflict. Spanish speakers tend to translate the Spanish version word for word (“make a blind eye”, “a sword of double edge”) or to change one word of the formula; this card recommends not overusing them in a formal register.
